All three clusters were attacked, leaving tiny pits on the surface, though the slime mold couldn't finish it all.

Remixed_Audio_Script: My parents constantly ruined my birthdays with sudden emergencies, so I eavesdropped and discovered the twisted truth. What exact moment made you despise your own birthday? Parents scrambled, the bouncy house was deflated, and I just sat on the steps in my party hat watching my dream birthday disappear. Dad spent three days in the hospital for a 'stomach infection,' and I felt horrible for caring about my party. After that year, every single birthday featured a crisis. At nine, my mom got sudden food poisoning an hour before my sleepover. At ten, grandma fell down the stairs at the bowling alley. At eleven, dad's appendix flared up right as guests arrived. At twelve, our car mysteriously broke down on the way to the amusement park. By thirteen, I gave up hope. I'd wake up with dread, waiting for the inevitable disaster. Friends stopped expecting invites. I tried begging for tiny, low-key dinners, but it didn't matter. The power would cut out, or dad would fake a hand injury. At sixteen, I begged for just a normal restaurant dinner. Halfway through the appetizers, my mom loudly claimed she was having heart palpitations, ensuring the whole restaurant heard. We left before the food even arrived. I actually started therapy at seventeen for extreme birthday anxiety. Then I turned eighteen. I planned to get a coffee alone and ignore the day. I came home early from school and heard my mom laughing on the phone in the dining room. She was talking to my aunt. 'Oh, her birthday? We already took care of that fake emergency this morning,' she chuckled. 'We've been doing the fake emergency routine for years. It works flawlessly and is way easier than paying for an expensive party.' My dad laughed from the kitchen. 'The fake hospital bills were the best part. Kept her from asking for big gifts!' I froze. Every ruined cake, every panic attack, every apology I made—it was all a calculated scam. I walked into the dining room, and they practically jumped out of their skin. 'So nobody was ever sick?' I asked. Dad started stammering about 'protecting me from disappointment,' while Mom turned on the fake tears. I asked to see a single real medical bill. Dad snapped, 'How dare you question us?' I didn't say another word. I went to my room, packed a duffel bag, grabbed my savings, and walked out of their lives forever.

So for his ninth, I planned a dedicated, simple party at a local park pavilion—just hot dogs, balloons, and a cheap cake. The day prior, I stopped by my parents to grab folding tables. My mom didn't let me ask. She slammed her mug down and declared, 'You need to postpone the party.' She claimed Dana's kids saw the balloons and felt 'less than.' Dana chimed in, demanding sensitivity because her husband had just left her. So apparently, my son’s birthday was canceled. I stared right at my mother. 'He is nine years old.' Mom warned me to never bring him around again. Dana called me dramatic. Dad told me to 'think it over.' I took screenshots of every message, created a folder named 'Evidence,' and shut off my phone. Mom marched in, Dana had her phone out recording, and dad trailed behind. My son grabbed my hand, terrified. Mom loudly announced, 'We warned you about the consequences!' Mom tried to guilt me with 'After everything we’ve done for you!' I fired back, 'After everything I have done for you.' I told them they tried to ruin my kid's day and that negotiations were over. Then I turned to the kids and yelled, 'Who wants hot dogs?!' The kids cheered, leaving my family standing there stunned. Instead, they just had fun. One cousin whispered, 'His parties are actually fun.' My son beamed. Dana heard it, glared at me, and hissed, 'Must be nice having everyone obsessed with you.' Mom tried to scold me, but Dana stormed off to the car with mom chasing her. Dad just stood there. That's when I realized the truth: my kid's joy was never the issue. The issue was that we proved we didn't need them to be a happy family.

I opened the PDF attachment to find a fully itemized list: flowers, catering, chairs, photography. The grand total? $35,463.89. Below it, my dad had written, 'Please settle this promptly.' I just stared at the screen. My wedding wasn't a gift; it was a literal bill. My husband read it, went dead quiet, and simply said, 'They offered. This is purely about control.'
